Act 1 of MacBeth begins with three witches entering with lightning and thunder.  They discuss where to meet MacBeth.  They decide to do so after the battle is done.  The witches make a famous statement, saying "foul is fair, and fair is foul."  Then, the witches disappear.  The king enters with a wounded captain.  The king stated that this bloody man helped set me free.  MacBeth and Banquo enter after their victory.  The witches appear to them, however; they don't look like women.  In fact, they don't look human at all!  They prophesy that MacBeth will become a noble of Cawdor and become king.  They told Banquo that he would not be king, but his children would be.  Eventually, Ross (a king's messanger) comes and calls MacBeth the thane of Cawdor.  MacBeth is confused, realizing that the witches cannot be bad, but also cannot be good.  MacBeth is now thinking about murder and is lost in thought.  The seed of ambition has been clearly planted.  Banquo notices MacBeth is uneasy.  He warns MacBeth not to trust the witches, suggesting that evil forces tell small truths to lure people into greater harm.  The king says that the Thane of Cawdor has been murdered.  Malcom is declared heir to the throne, blocking MacBeth's path to the throne.  The king plans to visit MacBeth's castle.  Lady MacBeth is reading a letter about the witches.  She plots to kill the king.  The king enters, saying the castle has a pleasant atmosphere.  MacBeth is afraid to kill the king, and Lady MacBeth calls him a coward.  MacBeth finally agrees to kill him.  Although Macbeth begins the play as a brave and loyal warrior, his ambition ultimately leads him to betray King Duncan and destroy his own sense of honor.

Before this happened, three witches were meeting to discuss when and where they should meet Macbeth. Essay: Act One begins with three witches who stand in an open place discussing their next meeting. The witches, who may be the three fates from Greek myth, say their next meeting will be after a conflict in an open field. They plan to meet Macbeth here before the three depart. Before departing, we see the words "fair is foul, foul is fair". Those words are repeated multiple times in the story, indicating a theme. We then meet King Duncan, who receives news of a bloody battle from a captain. Duncan asks for more details from this battle, and Duncan gets news that Macdonwald betrayed the Scots for their opponents (the Norwegians). Angered by this, he orders Macdonwald's trial and execution, and orders a man named Ross to go to Macbeth. Macbeth, due to his loyalty to the Scots, was to be given Macdonwald's title of "Thane of Cawdor". The point of view shifts back to the witches, who come upon Banquo and Macbeth. Before departing, they announce that Macbeth would be Thane of Cawdor and eventually king. These events happen before Ross finds Macbeth to tell him about Macdonwald's fate, and how Macbeth is now Thane of Cawdor. With the peculiarity of this situation, Banquo and Macbeth at first refuse to believe these witches, until Ross shows up and gives them the news of Macbeth being Thane. In these scenes, we see the theme of predestination vs free will show up, and how our lives may already be fated. Essay:
In Act 1 of Macbeth, Shakespeare introduces the main characters, themes, and conflicts of the play. The play opens with the witches, who are key characters in the story. They begin by saying a phrase that curses and captures the meaning of the story: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair.” The witches also make plans to meet with Macbeth and tell him his “fate.” Later on, we are introduced to Macbeth and Banquo, who are presented as great and noble warriors of Scotland. When the witches meet them, they tell the two noblemen three prophecies: Macbeth will become Thane of Cawdor and then king, and Banquo’s sons will be kings. Soon after, Macbeth learns that he has been made Thane of Cawdor. Although Macbeth had already been named Thane of Cawdor, he was not aware of it yet, and this leads him to listen more closely to the witches’ prophecies for his life. Afterward, Macbeth and Banquo talk, and Banquo tells Macbeth that he does not trust the witches. After they finish talking, they are invited to King Duncan’s castle, where Duncan informs Macbeth that he will visit his castle to honor him. Macbeth, tormented by thoughts of becoming king, realizes this is his perfect opportunity to kill the king, but he knows the act would be evil. Macbeth sends a letter to his wife, Lady Macbeth, and once she reads it, she pushes Macbeth to act by verbally insulting his masculinity, which shows that Lady Macbeth is more ruthless and dominant than Macbeth. By the end of Act 1, Macbeth is conflicted about the plan, but he begins to take small steps toward murdering King Duncan.

Throughout class, we discussed four major points from Act 1. One of these points is the idea of “fair is foul, and foul is fair,” which becomes a major theme throughout the play. At the beginning, the witches curse the play with this statement, and we see this curse come to life through the conflict in Macbeth’s mind. The witches confuse Macbeth and make it unclear what is good and what is evil. Macbeth knows murder is wrong, but he believes killing King Duncan is the only way to become king. Another important point is the role of the witches themselves, as they embody chaos and darkness. Their purpose is to torment Macbeth by planting dark ideas in his mind, which eventually leads to his downfall. We also discussed Lady Macbeth’s influence on Macbeth because she is more determined and manipulative, and she believes Macbeth is too kind to seize the crown on his own. Lastly, we talked about Macbeth’s ambition; at first, Macbeth appears loyal and honorable, but once the witches plant their ideas in his mind, his ambition begins to take control. Although Macbeth has not committed any crimes yet, his willingness to imagine murder shows how easily ambition can corrupt him

Act 1 of Macbeth is very important for the setup of the story, and it all begins in scene 1 with the three witches meeting in the thunder and lightning. Here, the three witches decide on when they want to meet with Macbeth: after the battle on the heath (barren land). After deciding this, they give a quote that becomes an axiom of the story: good is bad and bad is good. In scene 2, the King and his son (Malcom) arrive to the battlefield to see a wounded captain who helped win the battle. When asked to tell his story, the captain sings the praises of Macbeth, basically attributing the whole of the battle's victory to Macbeth's heroism. According to him, the battle was not going in their favor and fortune was smiling on the enemy. However, Macbeth disdained this fake Fortune and cut the enemy (Macdonwald) apart. Their leader was killed, but the enemy came back with reinforcements. Then, the Thane of Ross arrived and tells an additional account of Macbeth's heroism, and this time it is mentioned that the Thane of Cawdor was a disloyal traitor. The king, pleased by Macbeth, decides than he will bestow upon him the title of Thane of Cawdor due to the upcoming execution of the current one. Scene 3 brings the story back to the three witches, but this time Macbeth and Banquo are there as well. Banquo, disgusted by what he sees, asks them what they are and why they are here. They proceed to give both Macbeth and Banquo prophecies. For Macbeth, they say that he will become Thane of Cawdor and later king. To Banquo, they say that he will be lesser yet happier, and that his descendants will be king. When they prompt the witches for more information, the witches dissapear. Right on cue, the Thane of Ross arrives to them to inform them of the king's decision to make Macbeth the Thane of Cawdor. Upon receiving this judgement, the two men become skeptical of the witches' prophecies. Banquo believes they should be cautious with following the prophecies, and Macbeth agrees (Macbeth has internal conflict about whether he should follow the prophecies or wait for them to come to him). Scene 4 brings the story back to the king and his son. Malcom informs the king that the Thane of Cawdor was executed, but that he died nobly. In his joy of Macbeth and the situation, the king declares Malcom as his new heir. Macbeth, having been tempted by the prophecy, sees this as a problem because to become king he needs to pass Malcom or get rid of him. In scene 5, Lady Macbeth is introduced. When she hears about this prophecy, she believes that Macbeth must kill the king to claim is rightful place. She then prays to be more cruel and shielded from God's view so that she and her husband can kill the king. When Macbeth arrives, she does her best to convince Macbeth they should kill him while he stays as their place. In Scene 6 the king and his party arrives and asks to meet Macbeth. The final scene, Scene 7, brings the story back to Lady Macbeth urging Macbeth to go through with the evil deed. He states that his willing to risk Heaven for being the king, but he does not want to bear the guilt because the king has been uncorrupt and good to him. So, he decides that he will not do it. However, Lady Macbeth chides him for being scared and says she is confident that they could pull it off. At last, Macbeth deliberates that he will go ahead with her and kill the king.

 

My reflection so far is that this Act has been a setup for the rest of the story, setting up the foundations for the themes to come. I also believe that it is ironic that Lady Macbeth is shown in such a cruel and "un-ladylike." The theme of the characters being clearly protrayed as good or bad (excluding the conflicted Macbeth) makes me think that the bad will survive while the good will die.
